issues.item: Checking Behind: I frequently look behind me to check if someone is following me
issues.explanation: The threat items 'Checking Behind' and 'Back to Wall' imply a persistent interpersonal pursuit/assault-style danger (someone following me, needing surveillance of the room) that is hard to reconcile with a life-threatening motor vehicle collision unless there is additional trauma content not represented elsewhere in the profile.

issues.item: Back to Wall: I feel unsafe unless my back is against a wall where I can see the room
issues.explanation: 'Institutional Failure' is not a natural fit with the rest of this MVC profile: the other items center on fragmented accident memory, mistrust of self/body, and hypervigilance, but this appraisal presupposes a salient protector/institution betrayal theme that is not supported by the trauma type or other selected items.

issues.item: Institutional Failure: The people or institutions that should have protected me let me down
issues.explanation: 'Avoid Social Contacts: Seeing people that I socialised with before the event' does not connect well to the represented triggers, memory, or appraisals. For an MVC case, avoidance is more coherently focused on travel, roads, vehicles, reminders of the crash, or internal trauma cues; avoidance of prior social contacts suggests a different maintaining process that is not otherwise represented.

vignette: Mr. Johnson is a 68-year-old widowed African man who has been a dancer for most of his life. Tragically, he was involved in a life-threatening motor vehicle collision several months ago. Since the accident, Mr. Johnson's life has been marked by a pervasive sense of unease and fragmented memories. On the day of the collision, Mr. Johnson was on his way to a dance rehearsal when another car swerved into his lane, causing a severe crash. The impact was jarring, and he remembers feeling disoriented and overwhelmed with fear as sirens approached. Despite receiving medical attention, the trauma has left deep emotional scars. Mr. Johnson struggles most with incomplete memories of the event. He feels like only parts of what happened are accessible to him, and when he tries to recall it deliberately, the memory is elusive. This difficulty in remembering leaves him feeling lost and confused about his own experience, which fuels his self-doubt. "I can't trust that I will do the right thing," he often tells himself. His body feels unreliable too; the collision left him with lingering pain and a sense of vulnerability. The fragmented nature of Mr. Johnson's memory has also influenced his maladaptive strategies. He avoids going out, preferring to stay at home where he feels safer. Even when he does venture outside, he finds it difficult to socialize with people he once enjoyed spending time with. The fear that he can't trust himself or his body makes him reluctant to engage in activities that were once a part of his daily routine. This self-doubt and sense of institutional failure (feeling let down by the systems meant to protect him) exacerbate his fears. When something takes longer than expected, Mr. Johnson assumes the worst is happening, putting him on high alert for any unexpected sounds or events that could trigger a flashback. "I feel unsafe unless my back is against a wall where I can see the room," he admits. Mr. Johnson's threat perceptions have become deeply intertwined with his maladaptive strategies. He avoids therapy content because discussing it makes him feel more vulnerable and unsure of how to proceed safely in the world. This avoidance reinforces his negative appraisals, creating a self-perpetuating cycle where each layer of fear feeds into another. Over time, Mr. Johnson’s life has become increasingly circumscribed by these fears. His occupation as a dancer is particularly affected; he can no longer participate in performances or rehearsals without intense anxiety. When he does attempt to go out, the slightest delay or unexpected sound triggers his hypervigilance, making it difficult for him to engage meaningfully with others. What frightens Mr. Johnson most is the uncertainty and lack of control over his own memories and experiences. He fears that he will never fully understand what happened and whether he can trust himself again. However, his current state has pushed him to seek help, driven by a hope that therapy might provide some clarity and a way to reclaim parts of his life. In conclusion, Mr. Johnson’s struggle is one of fragmented memories and overwhelming fears, where each layer of trauma feeds into the next, creating a complex web of negative appraisals, maladaptive strategies, and heightened threat perceptions. His journey to recovery will involve addressing these interwoven layers in a way that allows him to regain trust in himself and his experiences.
